Foundations: Thinking and Positioning Like a Consultant

Consulting is paid problem solving: a client pays for a clearer diagnosis, a credible plan and a measurable result. This module shows you how to turn your expertise into a sharp offer, how professional consultants break big problems into answerable questions, and where paying clients are found in Nigeria, across Africa and remotely.
What clients actually buy: problem, outcome and method
Explain how consulting differs from freelancing, training and employment

A consultant is paid to help a client make a better decision or fix a defined problem. The client owns the business and the final decision; the consultant brings a structured way of finding out what is really wrong, a recommendation, and often support while the change is made. This is different from **freelancing**, where the client usually asks for a defined output (a logo, a set of posts, a website), and from **training**, where you build other people's skills. Many consultants do all three, but they price and sell them differently.

You also need to decide early whether you sell **advisory** work (diagnose and recommend) or **implementation** work (stay and help make the change). Advisory work is shorter and easier to scope. Implementation support usually earns more and produces stronger case studies, because you can show the result, but it ties up more of your time and depends on the client's team doing their part.
What the client is really buying
**Confidence that the problem is understood.** Clients hire people who describe their problem more clearly than they can.
**A credible method.** A named, repeatable way of working (for example, a four-week review with three clear stages) feels safer than general expertise.
**A result they can see.** Fewer errors, faster processing, more paying customers, a registration approved, a decision made with evidence.

Notice what is missing: years of experience on their own. Experience matters, but only when it is translated into a problem you solve and an outcome you can help produce. This is why "I help businesses grow" rarely wins work. A busy owner cannot tell whether it fits her problem, and no friend can refer you with confidence.

The positioning statement

A simple formula works well: **I help [specific client] who [specific problem] to [measurable outcome] through [named method].** Keep it to one or two sentences. Use the words your clients use, not technical language. Then run three tests. The **stranger test**: could someone who has never met you say exactly what you do? The **referral test**: could a friend forward it to the right person in one WhatsApp message? The **measurement test**: is the outcome something a client could check before and after?
Worked example: from banker to consultant
For example, Funmi spent 12 years in bank operations in Ibadan. Her first statement was: "I help businesses with operations and finance."
She lists problems she has personally fixed: reconciliation backlogs, cash shortages at tills, slow loan approval files.
She asks which of these small institutions struggle with most. Three cooperative officers she knows all mention unreconciled member accounts.
She picks one client group: cooperative societies and microfinance banks in the South-West.
She defines the outcome: member accounts reconciled within 2 working days instead of weeks.
She names her method: a four-week "Clean Books Review" with a diagnosis week, a process redesign fortnight and a handover week.

New statement: "I help cooperatives and microfinance banks in the South-West clear reconciliation backlogs and keep member accounts reconciled within 2 working days, through a four-week Clean Books Review." It passes all three tests.
A niche is a front door, not a cage
Choosing one client group and one problem does not stop you taking other work. It gives people a clear reason to remember and refer you. You can add a second offer once the first one is winning work.
Outcomes must be measurable

Clients and consultants often disagree at the end of a job because "success" was never defined. Borrow the SMART idea used in goal setting: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. "Improve customer service" is not measurable. "Reply to every WhatsApp enquiry within 2 hours during opening times by the end of March" is. You will use this again when you write proposals in Module 3.
Consultants are paid to improve a client's decision or fix a defined problem, not just to share knowledge.

Structured problem solving: the key question, issue trees and hypotheses
Turn a vague client complaint into one clear key question
Build a MECE issue tree that breaks the question into parts you can test
Use a hypothesis to focus your analysis and avoid wasted work
Run simple arithmetic on an issue tree to find where the problem sits

Clients rarely describe their problem precisely. They say "sales are bad" or "staff are not serious". The first professional skill of a consultant is to turn that complaint into **one key question** that is specific, has a time frame and leads to a decision. For example: "What should Ade Pharmacy change in the next six months to bring monthly profit back to its 2025 level?"
A person standing at a fork with several options in front of her
A good key question tells you which decision the client must make at the end.
Issue trees and MECE

An **issue tree** breaks the key question into smaller questions, and those into smaller ones, until each branch can be answered with data or interviews. Good trees are **MECE**, short for Mutually Exclusive and Collectively Exhaustive. Mutually exclusive means branches do not overlap, so you do not count the same cause twice. Collectively exhaustive means together they cover every possible cause, so nothing important hides outside the tree.

The easiest MECE trees follow arithmetic. Profit equals revenue minus costs. Revenue equals number of customers times average spend per customer. Costs split into cost of goods and operating costs (rent, salaries, power, transport). Because these are formulas, the branches cannot overlap and nothing is left out.

Worked example: finding where the profit went
For example, a two-branch pharmacy in Lagos says profit has collapsed. The consultant collects one month from last year and the same month this year (all figures approximate, in naira).
Last year: 3,000 receipts at an average of 6,000 naira = 18,000,000 naira revenue. This year: 2,900 receipts at 6,500 naira = 18,850,000 naira. Revenue actually rose by 850,000 naira.
Cost of goods last year was 12,600,000 naira (70% of revenue). This year it is 14,140,000 naira, which is about 75% of revenue.
Operating costs rose from 3,600,000 to 4,000,000 naira, an increase of 400,000 naira.
If cost of goods had stayed at 70% of this year's revenue, it would be 13,195,000 naira, so the higher share explains about 945,000 naira of the 1,090,000 naira drop.
Most of the problem sits in the cost-of-goods branch, not sales. The consultant now focuses on supplier prices, expired stock and stock losses instead of advertising.

Working with hypotheses

A **hypothesis** is a best guess you set out to prove or disprove, for example "Stock is being lost between the warehouse and the second branch". It is not a conclusion. Writing it down early stops you collecting every possible piece of data. For each hypothesis, ask: what evidence would prove it, and what would disprove it? In the pharmacy, a stock count compared with the delivery notes for two weeks would test the stock-loss hypothesis quickly.
Do not fall in love with your first guess

The danger of hypotheses is confirmation bias: noticing only evidence that agrees with you. Always write down what result would prove you wrong, and share disproved hypotheses with the client too. It shows honesty and saves them money.
Prioritise the branches

You rarely have time to test every branch. Rank them by two things: how big the effect could be in naira or time, and how easy it is to test. Start with branches that are both large and quick to check. Explain this choice to the client so they understand why some questions are left for later.

Share a simple version of the tree with the client early. It shows how you are thinking, invites them to add causes you missed, and makes later findings easier to accept because they helped shape the questions.

Different clients buy consulting in very different ways. A shop owner decides in one conversation. A large company or a donor-funded programme follows a written procurement process that can take weeks. Knowing how your target client buys tells you what documents to prepare, how long a sale takes and how you will be paid.

Your clients may be on your street, across West Africa or in another time zone.

Larger buyers will usually ask for documents before they can pay you. Prepare them before you start marketing: registration with the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC), either as a business name or a limited company; a tax identification number; a business bank account in the registered name; and a one or two page **capability statement** listing your services, your method, two or three short examples of past work and your contact details. Some buyers also ask for references, so agree in advance with two former managers or clients that they will speak for you.
Reading Terms of Reference

In the development sector, assignments are often advertised with **Terms of Reference (ToR)**. A ToR describes the background, objectives, scope, expected deliverables, timeline, required qualifications and how proposals will be scored. An **Expression of Interest (EOI)** request asks you to show you are qualified before you are invited to submit a full proposal. Read the evaluation criteria first: if 40% of the marks go to "relevant experience" and you have none in that sector, partner with someone who has it or let that one pass.
**Objectives**: what the client wants to know or change.
**Scope**: geography, number of sites, period covered.
**Deliverables**: inception report, data collection tools, draft and final reports, presentation.
**Level of effort**: the number of consultant days the client expects, which helps you check your budget.
**Evaluation criteria**: how marks are shared between methodology, experience and price.
Choosing where to compete

Score each possible market on two questions, each from 1 to 5. **Value**: how much does this client group lose from the problem, and can they pay? **Winnability**: do you have experience, contacts, documents and proof that this group trusts? Keep it simple: place each market on the matrix below and start where both scores are high.

Worked example: choosing a first market
For example, Chiamaka is a public health nurse with 10 years of community programme experience in Enugu. She considers three markets.
Private clinics wanting better patient records: value 3, winnability 2 (few contacts). Total picture: low priority.
NGOs running maternal health programmes needing baseline surveys: value 4, winnability 4 (she has run household surveys and knows two programme managers).
State health agency projects: value 5, winnability 1 (no registered company, no public procurement record).
She places NGOs in the "start here" box and the state agency in "build towards".
She sets up job alerts on NGO job boards and sends her CV with two survey examples to the two programme managers.
Chiamaka has one clear first market, a reason for choosing it, and a longer-term target she will build towards once she has a registered company and two strong case studies.
Working with remote clients safely

Much consulting work, especially research, analysis, report writing and advisory calls, can be done remotely. Agree meeting times in both time zones in writing, use shared folders such as Google Drive, and send short written summaries after each call. For payment, use channels you can verify, such as a domiciliary account or an established payment platform, and take a deposit before starting.
Protect yourself and client data

Never pay a "registration fee" to receive a consulting contract; real clients do not charge you to hire you. Do not send your BVN, card details or one-time codes to anyone. When a client shares personal data (staff, members, patients), keep it in secure, password-protected folders and use it only for the agreed purpose, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023.
Each buyer group has its own buying process, documents and payment habits.

This module gives you the working kit of a professional consultant: the diagnostic tools that find root causes, the phases and workplan that keep an engagement on track, and the way to turn analysis into clear, checked recommendations a client can act on.

Consultants do not need expensive software. Most diagnostic work uses a spreadsheet (Google Sheets or Excel), a survey or data-collection tool (Google Forms, or KoboToolbox for field surveys on phones), a shared folder, and a few well-chosen thinking tools. This lesson covers four tools you will use in almost every engagement. Each one answers a different question, so choose the tool that fits the branch of your issue tree.

Process mapping

A **process map** shows each step from the moment work starts (an order arrives) to the moment it ends (the customer is paid or served). Draw it with the people who actually do the work, not only the manager, because the real process is often different from the official one. Mark three things on each step: how long it takes, how long work waits before the step, and how often it goes wrong. Waiting time is usually much larger than working time, and that is where improvements hide.

The **Pareto principle**, often called the 80/20 rule, is the common pattern that a small number of causes produce most of the effects. It is a pattern to check, not a law: the split may be 70/30 or 90/10. To test it, count problems by category, sort from largest to smallest, and add a running total percentage.
Worked example: Pareto analysis of delivery complaints
For example, a parcel delivery company in Port Harcourt logged 400 customer complaints over three months and asks why customers are leaving.
Count by type: late delivery 180, wrong address handling 90, damaged parcel 50, rider attitude 40, payment problems 25, other 15. Total 400.
Work out each share: late 180 / 400 = 45%; wrong address 90 / 400 = 22.5%; damaged 50 / 400 = 12.5%.
Running total: 45% after late delivery, 67.5% after adding wrong address, 80% after adding damaged parcels.
In Google Sheets, sort the counts in descending order, use =B2/SUM($B$2:$B$7) for each share and a running SUM for the cumulative column, then insert a combo chart.
Conclusion: three of the six categories explain 80% of complaints, so the engagement focuses on dispatch timing, address capture and packaging.
Instead of a general customer service campaign, the client works on three specific causes. Rider attitude still matters, but it is not where most complaints come from.
The 5 Whys

Ask "why?" about a problem, then ask "why?" about the answer, usually around five times, until you reach a cause the client can actually change. Write down the evidence for each answer. If an answer is a guess, mark it and check it before moving on.
5 Whys for late deliveries
Parcels arrive late
Riders leave the hub after 11am
Parcels are sorted mid-morning
Online orders arrive overnight unsorted
No night sorting shift exists
The root cause is a missing sorting step, not slow riders, so the fix is a schedule change.
A person is rarely the root cause

If your 5 Whys ends with "the staff are lazy", keep going. Ask why the process allows the mistake, why training did not prevent it, or why the incentive points the wrong way. Blaming individuals hurts trust and usually leaves the real cause in place.
Stakeholder mapping

Change succeeds or fails through people. List everyone affected by your work: owners, managers, staff, customers, regulators, funders. Place each one on a grid by **influence** (can they approve, block or slow the change?) and **interest** (how much does the change affect them?). Manage high-influence, high-interest people closely with regular meetings. Keep high-influence, low-interest people satisfied with short updates. Keep high-interest, low-influence people informed, because they are often the staff whose daily work will change.
Close partners: the owner, the operations manager. Meet weekly.
Keep satisfied: the bank that funds the business. Share a one-page summary at key milestones.
Keep informed: dispatch staff and riders. Involve them in the process map and test new schedules with them.
Monitor: suppliers with little stake in the change.

Use these tools together. In the delivery example, the process map showed where parcels waited, the Pareto analysis showed which complaints mattered most, the 5 Whys explained why parcels waited, and the stakeholder map showed who had to agree to a night shift. Record which tool produced each finding so the client can follow your reasoning.
Pick the tool that matches the question: process map, Pareto, 5 Whys or stakeholder map.
Waiting time between steps is often where the biggest improvement hides.
Pareto analysis needs counts by category, a sort and a running total.
Keep asking why until you reach a cause the client can change, not a person to blame.
Run a Pareto analysis

Enter the categories and counts in Google Sheets and sort them from largest to smallest.
Add a share column and a running total column using formulas.
Mark the categories that together reach about 80%.
Write a 5 Whys chain for the largest category.

Clients judge consultants on how the work is run as much as on the final report. A clear structure tells the client what is happening each week, what you need from them and when decisions will be made. Most engagements, whatever the subject, follow four phases.
A small team planning work together around a board
A shared workplan keeps the consultant and the client's team moving together.

Start-up and inception
Diagnose
Design solutions
Deliver and hand over
Each phase ends with an output the client reviews before the next phase starts.
Phase
Main activities
Output the client sees
Kick-off meeting, data request, agree contacts and meeting rhythm

The kick-off meeting
Restate the key question and the agreed outcome, and ask the client to confirm or correct them.
Confirm scope: what is included and what is not.
Name one client contact person who can open doors, share data and book staff time.
Hand over a written data request with dates (for example: 18 months of sales records by Friday).
Agree the meeting rhythm, such as a 30-minute weekly check-in and a review meeting at the end of each phase.
Ask about sensitivities: people, past consultants, or topics to handle carefully.

Within a few days, send a short **inception note** (one to three pages) that records these agreements. In donor-funded work this is often a formal **inception report** listed as a deliverable in the Terms of Reference. Either way, it protects both sides: if the scope changes later, you can point to what was agreed.
The workplan and consultant days

Plan your effort in **consultant days** (also called person-days or level of effort). A day is one person working a full working day. Listing days by activity shows whether the plan fits the budget and the calendar, and reveals if you are trying to do too much.
Worked example: a six-week workplan
For example, Halima agrees a six-week operations review for a cooperative in Kano with a level of effort of 20 consultant days.
Week 1, start-up: kick-off, data request and inception note: 2 days.
Weeks 2 and 3, diagnose: 12 staff interviews at about half a day each including notes (6 days) plus data analysis (3 days): 9 days.
Week 4, design: preparing and running an options workshop: 3 days.
Week 5, draft report: 4 days. Week 6, final report and handover meeting: 2 days.
Total: 2 + 9 + 3 + 4 + 2 = 20 days, which matches the agreed effort.
Check the calendar: 20 days over 6 weeks is about 3.3 days a week, leaving Halima time for other clients and travel.
Halima's plan fits the effort and the calendar. When the client later asks for 10 more interviews, she can show it would add about 5 days and needs a change request.
Roles and status reporting

Use a simple **RACI** list for each major task: who is Responsible for doing it, who is Accountable for approving it, who must be Consulted and who should be Informed. For example, for the data request the client's finance officer is responsible, the owner is accountable, and the consultant is consulted.

Every week, send a short written update by email or WhatsApp. Use a **RAG rating**: Green means on track, Amber means at risk but recoverable, Red means a deadline or outcome will be missed without a decision. Keep it to five lines: overall rating, done this week, planned next week, what you need from the client, risks.
Bad news early is good service

If data arrives late, say so in the status update the same week, with the impact on dates and what you need. Clients forgive delays they hear about early. They rarely forgive surprises in the final week.
Closing the engagement

End every engagement on purpose rather than letting it fade away. Hold a **handover meeting** where you walk through the final deliverables, confirm who owns each recommendation and agree when you will check progress, for example 30 and 90 days later. Then send a short **close-out note** that lists what was delivered against the inception note, any open items, the final invoice and how to reach you. This note is also the moment to ask whether the client would be willing to give feedback or a reference.

From analysis to recommendations: the pyramid principle, quality checks and confidentiality
Structure findings with Situation, Complication, Question and Answer
Build a pyramid of one main message, supporting arguments and evidence
Write recommendations that state what, who, by when, cost and expected result
Run a quality and confidentiality check before anything reaches the client

A busy client reads the first page and perhaps the headings. If your main message is buried on page 14, it may never be read. Professional consultants therefore put the answer first and then show why it is right. A widely used method for this is the **pyramid principle**, described by Barbara Minto, a former McKinsey consultant, in her book *The Minto Pyramid Principle*.
A woman presenting a chart to an audience
Lead with the answer, then support it with a few clear arguments and evidence.
Start with SCQA
**Situation**: what the client already knows and agrees with.
**Complication**: what has changed or gone wrong.
**Question**: the question this creates (often your key question).
**Answer**: your main recommendation, in one or two sentences.
The pyramid of a recommendation
One main recommendation
Three supporting arguments
Evidence for each argument
Every argument must support the message above it, and every piece of evidence must support its argument.
Worked example: rewriting a weak finding

For example, after the delivery company review in Port Harcourt, the first draft summary read: "We conducted interviews and analysed data. Several issues were found in dispatch, addressing and packaging. Recommendations are in section 6."
Situation: the company has grown quickly and now handles most orders from online shops.
Complication: complaints have risen, and three categories (late, wrong address, damaged) make up 80% of the 400 complaints logged in three months.
Question: what should the company change first to cut complaints?
Answer: start a night sorting shift, require a landmark and phone-confirmed address at order entry, and introduce a standard padded pack for fragile items.
Each of the three actions becomes a supporting argument, with the Pareto chart, the 5 Whys chain and interview quotes as evidence.
The client reads the answer in the first paragraph, sees why in three short sections and can approve the actions in one meeting.
The "so what?" test and action titles

For every chart or table, ask "so what?" until you reach the point for the client. Then make that point the title. A weak slide title says "Complaints by category". An **action title** says "Three causes create 80% of complaints". When you read only the titles of a good deck, you should understand the whole story.

Presenting findings without surprises

Before a big findings meeting, share the main messages privately with the key stakeholders from your stakeholder map. Consultants call this **pre-wiring**. It lets people raise objections in private, correct facts you may have wrong, and arrive at the meeting already familiar with the conclusions. A manager who first hears in front of colleagues that her department causes most of the delays will defend herself rather than discuss solutions.

In the meeting itself, state the main message in the first two minutes, then walk through the supporting arguments. When someone disagrees, ask what evidence would change their view, and offer to check it. Record decisions and open questions in a short note sent the same day.
Keep the slides or report short. A findings deck for a small business is often ten to fifteen slides, with detailed tables moved to an appendix.
Quality checks before you send
Numbers tie out: totals add up, percentages match counts, and the same figure is identical everywhere it appears.
Every claim has a source: a dataset, an interview, a document. Mark estimates clearly.
The client's name, people's titles and dates are correct.
A second person reads it, ideally someone who has not seen the work, and tells you the main message in their own words.
File names show version and date, for example ClientName_Report_v3_2026-03-14, so nobody comments on an old draft.

Keep an **engagement file** for every client: the signed letter, the inception note, an interview log (who, when, main points), your analysis workbook with the raw data kept on a separate tab, a decisions log and each version of the deliverables. If a client later questions a number, you can show exactly where it came from, and the file becomes the raw material for your case study.
Confidentiality and data protection

Interview notes, salaries and customer lists are confidential. Store them in password-protected folders, share only with people named in the agreement, and remove names from quotes unless the person agreed. Keep personal data only as long as the engagement needs it, in line with the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023, and never reuse a client's data or documents for another client.

Clients, Pricing, Leadership and Your Consulting Portfolio

Now you bring everything to the client: discovery conversations that find and cost the real problem, fees and engagement letters that protect both sides, and case studies and a 90-day plan that turn finished work into the next engagement.
Client discovery: questions that uncover the real problem and its cost

A **discovery meeting** is the conversation before any proposal. Its purpose is not to sell. It is to understand the client's situation well enough to decide whether you can help and, if so, what a sensible engagement looks like. Clients often decide to hire you during discovery, because good questions show expertise better than any brochure.
Two people in a structured conversation across a table
In discovery, the client should talk for most of the meeting while you listen and take notes.
Before the meeting
Read the client's website, social pages and any public news so you do not ask what you could have looked up.
Write three hypotheses about what might be wrong, using an issue tree from Module 1.
Prepare an agenda and send it ahead: introductions (5 minutes), their situation (20), goals and constraints (10), next steps (10).
Confirm who will attend. If the decision maker is not coming, ask whether they can join for the last 10 minutes.
A discovery question bank
Area
Example questions
Situation
Walk me through how this works today. When did you first notice the problem?
Impact
What does this cost you each month in money, time or customers? Who feels it most?
Past attempts
What have you already tried? What happened? Have you worked with a consultant before, and what did you like or not like?
Desired outcome
If we meet in six months and this is solved, what will be different? How will you measure it?
Constraints
What budget range have you set aside? Are there deadlines, such as a board meeting or funding round?
Decision process
Who else needs to agree before work starts? How do you usually approve a supplier?

Listen more than you speak. Repeat back what you heard in your own words ("So the main issue is that parents pay late, and it hits salaries in week three?") and let the client correct you. Note exact phrases the client uses; you will reuse them in your proposal so it reads as their problem, not your theory.

Avoid offering solutions during discovery, even when you can see one. Early advice is often wrong because you have only heard part of the story, and it gives away the value the client should be paying for.
Put a number on the problem
Worked example: costing late school fees
For example, the proprietor of a private primary school in Abuja says "parents are not paying". In discovery the consultant asks for the numbers (all figures approximate).
The school has 420 pupils and an average fee of 350,000 naira per term, so termly billing is 420 x 350,000 = 147,000,000 naira.
By the end of the term, 18% of fees are still unpaid: 147,000,000 x 0.18 = 26,460,000 naira outstanding.
The proprietor says a well-run school she admires keeps unpaid fees at about 5%. At 5%, outstanding fees would be 147,000,000 x 0.05 = 7,350,000 naira.
The gap is 26,460,000 minus 7,350,000 = 19,110,000 naira per term that could be collected on time.
She adds that late salaries have caused two teachers to resign this year, a cost that is real but harder to count.
Both sides now see that the problem is worth about 19 million naira per term in cash flow, plus staff losses. This shapes the scope, the fee and how success will be measured.

Strong discovery gives you everything you need for a proposal the client will recognise.
Decide: propose, refer or walk away

After the meeting, check five things: Is the problem clear? Is it worth solving (its cost is clearly larger than your likely fee)? Does the person you met have authority, or access to it? Is there a realistic budget and timing? Is it within your real expertise? If all five are yes, write the proposal. If the problem is outside your expertise, refer the client to someone better suited; it protects your reputation and often brings referrals back.
Red flags in discovery

Be careful when a client wants a fixed price before sharing any information, asks you to promise a result you cannot control (for example a guaranteed grant or contract), refuses to involve the decision maker, or asks you to hide information from staff, partners or regulators. Each is a reason to slow down, put conditions in writing or decline.
Follow up within 24 hours

Send a short email or WhatsApp message within a day. Thank the client, summarise the problem in their own words, restate the cost you calculated together, list what you agreed would happen next (for example, a proposal by Thursday) and ask for any data they promised. This summary often becomes the opening section of your proposal, and it shows the client that you listened carefully.
Discovery is for understanding, not selling; the client should talk most.
Prepare hypotheses and an agenda, and get the decision maker involved.
Always cost the problem in naira or time before you price your work.
Propose only when the problem, value, authority, budget and fit are all clear.

Pricing models, value-based fees and the engagement letter
Compare day-rate, fixed project, value-based and retainer pricing

Present three scoped options with clear payment milestones
Draft the key clauses of an engagement letter, including change requests

Pricing is where many skilled consultants lose money. They either charge too little because they only count hours, or they lose good clients by quoting a large number with no link to the client's problem. A professional fee is built from two sides: what the work costs you to deliver, and what the result is worth to the client.
A signed contract with a pen and a check mark
A clear fee and a signed engagement letter come before any work starts.
Model
How it works
Best for
Watch out for
Day rate
Client pays for each consultant day used
Open-ended advisory work, donor contracts that specify days
Income stops when you work faster
Fixed project fee
One price for a defined scope and deliverables
Clearly scoped reviews and projects
Scope creep if exclusions are vague
Value-based fee
Price set with reference to the value of the result to the client
Problems with a clear naira value
Needs trust and good discovery numbers

Monthly fee for agreed ongoing access or tasks
Ongoing advice after a project
Define what is included each month
Step 1: know your day rate

Start with the income you need for the year, add your business costs (data, transport, software, phone, accountant), and divide by the days you can realistically bill. Consultants spend many days on selling, admin and learning, so billable days are much lower than working days.
Worked example: from day rate to a project fee and a value check
For example, Ngozi is pricing the school fees engagement from the previous lesson. All naira figures are approximate and for illustration only.
She needs 21,000,000 naira of personal income in a year and expects 3,000,000 naira of business costs: 24,000,000 naira in total.
She expects about 230 working days but only about 120 billable days after selling, admin and holidays. Day rate: 24,000,000 / 120 = 200,000 naira.
Her workplan for the school is 18 days. Cost-based fee: 18 x 200,000 = 3,600,000 naira. She adds 10% for risk: 3,600,000 x 1.10 = 3,960,000 naira, rounded to 4,000,000 naira.
Value check: the problem is worth about 19,110,000 naira per term in fees collected on time. 4,000,000 / 19,110,000 is about 21% of one term's improvement, and the benefit repeats every term.
She is confident the fee is fair and easy to justify, and she does not discount it.
Ngozi quotes 4,000,000 naira for the core option, explained in terms of the client's own numbers rather than her hours.
Step 2: offer three options

Give the client a choice of scope, not a choice of discount. For example: **Option A, Diagnose** (review and recommendations only, 2,500,000 naira); **Option B, Diagnose and design** (adds new fee policy, reminder scripts and Paystack payment links set up with staff, 4,000,000 naira); **Option C, Implement** (adds two months of monthly check-ins and a staff training session, 5,500,000 naira). Most clients choose the middle option, and every option is profitable for you.

Agree **payment milestones**, for example 50% on signing and 50% on the final deliverable, or 40% on signing, 40% on the findings review and 20% on handover. Never start without the first payment. If you are registered for VAT, show it separately; ask a qualified tax adviser how VAT and any withholding tax apply to your fees.
Step 3: the engagement letter
**Parties and dates**: who is contracting, start and end dates.
**Objectives and scope**: the key question, what is included and, just as important, what is excluded.
**Deliverables**: each output with a format and due date.
**Client responsibilities**: data, staff time, a contact person, response times for reviews.
**Fees and payment**: amount, milestones, how to pay, what happens if payment is late.
**Change requests**: how extra work is agreed and priced.
**Confidentiality and data**: how client information is stored, used and returned or deleted.
**Ownership**: who owns the final report and any templates you bring.
**Termination**: how either side can end the contract and what is paid for work done.
Handling a change request
Client asks for extra work
Check against agreed scope
Estimate days, fee, dates
Client approves in writing
Update workplan and invoice
Every addition goes through the same steps, so goodwill never turns into unpaid work.
Get legal help for large contracts

A clear engagement letter is enough for most small engagements. For large contracts, government work or international clients, ask a lawyer to review the terms, especially liability, ownership of work and termination.

Finally, review your pricing after every few engagements. Compare the days you planned with the days you actually worked. If you keep running over, either your estimates are too low or your scope is too loose, and both can be fixed before the next proposal.
Build the fee from your cost to deliver, then test it against the client's value.
Offer three scoped options, not discounts.
Use payment milestones and never start before the first payment.
A written engagement letter with exclusions and a change process prevents most disputes.

Your next client will trust evidence more than claims. A short, specific **case study** that shows a real problem, your method and a measured result is the strongest marketing a consultant can have. If you are new, run one well-scoped engagement at a reduced fee or as a structured pro bono project, on the condition that you can measure results and publish an anonymised case study.
A person arranging work samples in a portfolio
Each finished engagement should leave you with a case study for the next client.
Structure of a consulting case study
Client context
The challenge
Your approach
Measured results
Lessons and quote
Keep each part short, and make the results section the one with the clearest numbers.
Worked example: a one-page case study
For example, after the Abuja school engagement, Ngozi writes a case study. The proprietor agrees, in writing, that the school can be described but not named.
Context: a private primary school in Abuja with 420 pupils.
Challenge: 18% of termly fees were unpaid at term end, about 26 million naira, causing late salaries and staff exits.
Approach: a six-week review: fee process map, a Pareto analysis of reasons for late payment, a new fee policy, reminder messages at set dates, and payment links for transfers.

Results: the following term, unpaid fees at term end fell to 7% of billing, about 10,290,000 naira (147,000,000 x 0.07), compared with 26,460,000 naira before: an improvement of about 16,170,000 naira.
Lessons and quote: the target of 5% was not yet reached; the next step is earlier reminders. The proprietor's quote is used with her permission.
An honest case study with a before and after figure, including the part not yet achieved, which makes it more believable to future clients.
Leading change with the client

Recommendations only matter if people act on them. Consultants lead without authority, so you lead through process. Run short, well-prepared workshops: send the purpose and pre-reading first, start with the evidence, let staff test and improve the options, and end with named owners and dates. People support what they help to build.
When staff resist, ask what worries them. Resistance often hides a real risk the plan has missed.
Run a small pilot (one branch, one class, one month) before a full rollout.
Agree two or three simple measures and review them at 30 and 90 days after handover.
Celebrate early results in front of the team, giving credit to the staff who made them happen.
Turning finished work into the next client

Most consulting work comes from referrals and repeat clients, so the end of an engagement is the start of your next sale. At the 30-day check-in, ask how the changes are going and whether the measures are moving. If the client is pleased, ask three specific questions: may I use this as an anonymised case study, would you give a short quote, and who else do you know who faces a similar problem? Specific requests get far better answers than "please refer me".

Consider offering a small **retainer** after the main project, such as a monthly review call and a short written check of the agreed measures. It keeps the improvements on track for the client and gives you steady income while you look for the next engagement.
Ethics that protect your reputation

Declare any conflict of interest, such as advising a client while also working for a competitor or earning commission from a supplier you recommend. Do not claim expertise you do not have; say so and refer. Report findings honestly, even when the person who hired you is part of the problem, and handle that conversation privately and respectfully. Keep client information confidential after the engagement ends.

What clients buy
Three things a client pays for
Confidence that you describe their problem more clearly than they can.
A named, repeatable way of working, for example a four-week review with three stages.
Fewer errors, faster processing, more paying customers, a decision made with evidence.
Clients hire people who describe their problem more clearly than they can.
A named method feels safer than general expertise.
And they want a result they can see. Notice what is missing: years of experience on their own. That is why I help businesses grow rarely wins work.
Positioning
From banker to consultant
I help [client] who [problem] to [outcome] through [method].
List problems you have personally fixed
Ask which ones clients struggle with most
Pick one client group
Define a measurable outcome
Name your method

Funmi spent 12 years in bank operations in Ibadan. Her first statement was: I help businesses with operations and finance. Too vague. So she lists problems she has fixed, like reconciliation backlogs and cash shortages at tills.
Three cooperative officers she knows all mention unreconciled member accounts.
She picks cooperatives and microfinance banks in the South-West.
Her outcome: member accounts reconciled within 2 working days instead of weeks.
Her method: a four-week Clean Books Review. Now test it. Could a stranger say what you do? Could a friend forward it in one WhatsApp message? Could a client check the outcome before and after?
Problem solving
Key question, issue tree, hypothesis
Turn the complaint into one key question
Split it into a MECE issue tree
Use formulas: profit = revenue minus costs
Test hypotheses, and say what proves you wrong
Clients say sales are bad, or staff are not serious. Turn that into one specific key question with a time frame, that leads to a decision.
Break it into an issue tree. Good trees are MECE: the branches do not overlap, and together they cover every possible cause.
The easiest trees follow arithmetic. Profit is revenue minus costs. Revenue is customers times average spend.
A hypothesis is a best guess you set out to prove or disprove. Write down what result would prove you wrong, so you do not notice only the evidence that agrees with you.
Worked example
Where did the pharmacy's profit go?
For example, a two-branch pharmacy in Lagos says profit has collapsed. This is one month this year.
Revenue
Cost of goods
Operating costs
Figures are approximate.
The consultant compares the same month last year, branch by branch of the tree.
Revenue is 18,850,000 naira. It actually rose by 850,000 naira, so sales are not the problem.
Cost of goods is 14,140,000 naira. That is about 75% of revenue, up from 70% last year.
Operating costs rose by 400,000 naira, to 4,000,000.

Profit fell from 1,800,000 to 710,000 naira. The higher cost-of-goods share explains about 945,000 of the 1,090,000 drop. So the consultant checks supplier prices, expired stock and stock losses, not advertising.
Choosing a market
Start where value and winnability meet
NGO maternal health surveys
Value 4, winnability 4
She knows two programme managers
State health agency projects
Value 5, winnability 1
No registered company yet

Score each market from 1 to 5 for value to the client, and for your ability to win. Chiamaka, a public health nurse in Enugu, has run household surveys and knows two programme managers. NGOs are her first market.
A state agency scores high on value, but she has no registered company or procurement record yet. She builds towards it.
Larger buyers expect CAC registration, a tax number, a business account and a short capability statement.
Safety first
Never pay a fee to receive a contract
Never send your BVN, card details or codes
Use payment channels you can verify
Take a deposit before starting
Keep client personal data secure
Real clients do not charge you to hire you, so never pay a registration fee for a contract. Never send your BVN, card details or one-time codes to anyone.
With remote clients, use verified payment channels and take a deposit. Keep any personal data in password-protected folders, and use it only for the agreed purpose.

Why this matters
The working kit of a consultant
Use simple tools to find root causes
Run the engagement in four clear phases
Put your answer first
Check quality and protect confidential data
You do not need expensive software. A spreadsheet, a survey tool, a shared folder and a few thinking tools are enough.
Clients judge you on how the work is run as much as on the final report.
A busy client reads the first page and perhaps the headings. If your main message is on page 14, it may never be read.
And every number must be checked before it reaches the client.
Diagnostic toolkit
Four tools, four questions
Process map: where does work slow down?
Pareto: which few causes make most problems?
5 Whys: what is the root cause?
Stakeholder map: who can block or support?
Draw a process map with the people who actually do the work, not only the manager. Mark how long each step takes and how long work waits. Waiting time is usually where improvements hide.
Pareto analysis checks the common pattern that a few causes produce most of the effects.
The 5 Whys keeps asking why until you reach a cause the client can change.
And a stakeholder map places people by influence and interest, because change succeeds or fails through people.
Worked example
Pareto: 400 delivery complaints
If your 5 Whys ends with a person to blame, keep going.
Count complaints by type
Sort from largest to smallest
Work out each share and a running total
Focus on the causes that reach about 80%
Ask 5 Whys about the biggest one
A parcel delivery company in Port Harcourt logged 400 complaints in three months. Late delivery 180, wrong address 90, damaged parcels 50, and smaller groups.
Sort them in Google Sheets, largest first.
Late delivery is 45%. Add wrong address and the running total is 67.5%. Add damaged parcels and it reaches 80%.
So three of the six categories explain 80% of complaints. The work focuses there, not on a general customer service campaign.
Why are parcels late? Riders leave the hub after 11am. Why? Parcels are sorted mid-morning. Why? Overnight orders arrive unsorted. Why? There is no night sorting shift.
The root cause is a missing step, not slow riders. Blaming individuals hurts trust and usually leaves the real cause in place.
Running the job
Four phases, one workplan
Start-up: kick-off and inception note
Diagnose: interviews, maps, data
Design: options workshop with the client
Deliver: final report and handover meeting
At kick-off, restate the key question, confirm scope, name one client contact, and hand over a written data request with dates. Then send a short inception note that records it all.
Plan effort in consultant days. Halima's six-week review in Kano has 20 days. 9 of them are for diagnosis: 12 staff interviews and data analysis.
Each phase ends with an output the client reviews. When the client asks for 10 more interviews, she shows it adds about 5 days, and needs a change request.
Every week, send a five-line update rated green, amber or red. Bad news early is good service. Clients rarely forgive surprises in the final week.
Recommendations
Weak and strong recommendations
Night sorting shift, two staff
First Monday of next month
Riders leave the hub by 8am
Put the answer first. Use Situation, Complication, Question, Answer, then three supporting arguments, each with evidence. This is the pyramid principle.
Give each chart an action title, like: three causes create 80% of complaints.

A strong recommendation says what, who, by when, the cost, and the expected result. Before the meeting, share the main messages privately with key people, so nobody is surprised in front of colleagues.
Quality and safety
Before anything reaches the client
Numbers tie out everywhere they appear
Every claim has a source; estimates marked
A second person repeats the main message
Confidential notes in protected folders
Names removed from quotes unless agreed
Check that totals add up and the same figure is identical everywhere. Mark estimates. Ask someone who has not seen the work to tell you the main message.
Interview notes, salaries and customer lists are confidential. Keep them in password-protected folders, share only with people named in the agreement, and never reuse one client's data for another.
Remember
What to keep from this module
Match the tool to the question
Look for causes the client can change
Plan in consultant days; report weekly
Answer first, then arguments and evidence
Remember. Match the tool to the question, and look for causes the client can change. Plan in consultant days and report every week. And always lead with the answer.

Discover the real problem, price it fairly, and win the next client.
This is the video for module three of Consulting Fundamentals.
Why this matters
Bring everything to the client
Run a discovery meeting that finds the real cost
Build a fee from your cost and the client's value
Protect both sides with an engagement letter
Turn finished work into the next engagement
A discovery meeting is not for selling. Good questions show your expertise better than any brochure.
Many skilled consultants lose money on pricing, because they only count hours.
A written letter with exclusions prevents most disputes.
And your next client will trust evidence more than claims.
Discovery
In discovery, the client talks most
Prepare three hypotheses and an agenda
Ask about impact, past attempts and budget
Repeat back what you heard
Do not offer solutions yet
Read about the client first, write three hypotheses, and send a short agenda. Make sure the decision maker joins, at least for the last 10 minutes.
Ask what the problem costs each month, what they already tried, and who else must agree before work starts.
Repeat back what you heard, in your own words, and note the client's exact phrases for your proposal.
Avoid offering solutions, even when you see one. You have only heard part of the story.
Within a day, send a summary of the problem in their words, the cost you calculated together, and the next steps.
Worked example
Costing late school fees
For example, a school proprietor in Abuja says parents are not paying. The consultant asks for the numbers.
Termly billing, 420 pupils
Unpaid at 18%
Unpaid at 5%
Figures are approximate.
Always put a number on the problem before you price your work.
420 pupils at an average of 350,000 naira per term is 147,000,000 naira.
18% is still unpaid at the end of term. That is 26,460,000 naira.
A well-run school she admires keeps unpaid fees at about 5%, which would be 7,350,000.
The gap is 19,110,000 naira per term, plus two teachers who resigned over late salaries. Now both sides know what the problem is worth.
Pricing
Build the fee from both sides
Never start work before the first payment.
Day rate = income need plus costs ÷ billable days
Fee = workplan days × day rate, plus risk
Check it against the value of the result
Agree payment milestones in writing
Ngozi needs 24,000,000 naira a year, including business costs. She expects only about 120 billable days, after selling, admin and holidays. So her day rate is 200,000 naira.
Her workplan for the school is 18 days, 3,600,000 naira. With 10% for risk, she rounds to 4,000,000.
That is about 21% of one term's improvement, and the benefit repeats every term. So she does not discount it.
She agrees milestones, for example 50% on signing and 50% on the final deliverable. Ask a qualified tax adviser how VAT and withholding tax apply to your fees.
Three options
Offer a choice of scope, not a discount
Review and recommendations only. 2,500,000 naira.
Adds a new fee policy, reminder scripts and payment links set up with staff. 4,000,000 naira.
Adds two months of check-ins and a staff training session. 5,500,000 naira.
Option A is diagnosis only, at 2,500,000 naira.
Option B adds the design work, at 4,000,000. Most clients choose the middle option.
Option C adds two months of support, at 5,500,000. Every option is profitable for you.
Engagement letter
What the letter must cover
Scope: what is included and excluded
Deliverables with due dates
Client responsibilities
Fees, milestones, late payment
Change requests and confidentiality

Your letter names the scope and, just as important, what is excluded. It lists deliverables, what the client must provide, fees and milestones, how extra work is priced, and how client information is stored and deleted.
For large or government contracts, ask a lawyer to review the terms.
Case study
An honest before and after
Before
18% of fees unpaid
About 26,460,000 naira
Late salaries, staff exits
After one term
7% of fees unpaid
About 10,290,000 naira
5% target not yet reached
Ngozi writes a one-page case study: context, challenge, approach, measured results, and lessons. The proprietor agrees in writing that the school can be described but not named.
Unpaid fees fell to 7%, an improvement of about 16,170,000 naira. She also says the 5% target was not yet reached. That honesty makes it more believable.
Declare any conflict of interest, and keep client information confidential after the job ends.
Your 90 days
Work backwards from your goal
Goal: 2 signed clients
6 proposals, if 1 in 3 is accepted
12 discovery meetings, if 1 in 2 leads on
60 outreach conversations, about 5 a week
Start with the number of clients you want, for example 2.
If 1 in 3 proposals is accepted, you need 6 proposals.
If 1 in 2 meetings leads to a proposal, you need 12 meetings.
And if 1 in 5 conversations leads to a meeting, you need 60, about 5 per week over 12 weeks. Track every stage weekly, and replace these estimates with your own numbers.
